paras: The lynching of C. A. Washington was the killing of a physician by a mob at Otero, New Mexico Territory, on the night of Thursday, December 2, 1880. Washington had been accused in the dying statement of a young hotel worker at Raton of drugging and assaulting her, and a mob that followed him from Raton took him from confinement and hanged him. Denver wire reports carried the story across the country, and Western papers presented the killing as deserved, while no report identified Washington as Black.

Washington had lived at Otero, a railroad station about fifteen miles south of the Colorado line, after earlier stays as a druggist at La Veta, Las Animas and El Moro, Colorado. According to Capt. Cutler of the Trinidad News, he had been driven from La Veta for abusing his wife, had been acquitted on a plea of self-defense in the knife killing of a partner, and had been suspected of killing his own infant. The Las Vegas Morning Gazette added that he had bought his medical title from the Kansas City Medical College, and several reports believed Washington was not his real name.

Called to Raton to treat a dining-room girl at a hotel, he attended her the night before she died on Wednesday, December 1. Before her death she said he had given her two large doses of a drug, chloroform in most accounts and morphine in the Denver dispatch, and had assaulted her while she was semi-conscious.

At Raton a 'band of vigilantes' formed at once, and the Gazette reported that only Officer Hogan and a cowboy prevented a lynching that Wednesday night by hurrying Washington off to Otero. In the Trinidad account the officials took him to Otero, where he was locked up, but the mob followed and arrived after nightfall on Thursday 'in large numbers.' The wire and Trinidad reports said the mob forced the doors of his prison, took him out and hanged him until he was strangled.

A later Gazette report, based on unnamed informants, said instead that the men took him from a saloon to the windmill, where he was hanged. The same report said he made no confession, believed his captors only wanted to force one, and told them he hoped they would be 'in better humor' when they met him in hell.

When the train left Otero the next day the body had not been buried; $629 was said to have been found on it, and his father-in-law had arrived at Raton to take charge of his effects. The Gazette learned that the authorities would make no investigation, judging it wise not to excite further what it called a justly incensed people. No report of an inquest over Washington, an arrest or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Las Vegas Morning Gazette, writing before the lynching, called Washington a 'lustful wretch' and a 'brute' and quoted public opinion that 'it is a pity he isn't hung.' A Denver Tribune special, sent east on December 4 and 5, ran in Chicago, Cheyenne, Wheeling and elsewhere under headlines such as 'Served Him Right' and 'A Fiend Hanged by a Mob.' A longer version of the dispatch, printed in Lancaster and Canton, recited his 'most unsavory' record, and the Denver Tribune later wrote that the world was fortunate his life had ended even at the hands of a mob.

Weekly roundups as far away as Oregon reduced the case to a single line, sometimes calling him an 'ex-Professor of the Kansas City Medical College' and one placing the lynching at Raton. These columns marked Black lynching victims of the same week as '(colored)' or 'a negro' but gave no race for Washington, and the Gazette described his black hair and beard while naming another man in its story as 'a colored man.' The case also ran in a German-language Cincinnati paper; no Black-press coverage is available for this year.

Reports differed on the dead woman's name, given as Abbie J. Sinel of Topeka by the Gazette, Mary Butler in the Denver dispatch and Alice Sivel in Indiana roundups, and on her hotel and the drug used. A Kansas City Times special named the victim 'Dr. C. A. Woodburn' and put the hanging at 9 o'clock on the morning of December 2, and one Indiana summary said Washington had been arrested and discharged before the mob took him from jail.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob took Washington from confinement at Otero and hanged or strangled him for the alleged drugging and assault of a patient (A4, A7, A8, A25).

A mob that came 'in large numbers' forced his prison open and hanged him, without legal process, in punishment for an alleged crime against a patient (A8, A25); the local paper said the authorities would not investigate (A7). Whether the victim was Black is not stated in any report, which bears on scope, not on the verdict.
The Las Vegas Morning Gazette (A1, A7), the Denver Tribune wire (A4, A8) and a separate Trinidad dispatch (A25) independently report the mob killing at Otero.

accounts.label: Las Vegas Morning Gazette (local)
accounts.gist: Vigilantes at Raton nearly lynched him Wednesday night; officers took him to Otero, where men took him from a saloon to the windmill; he made no confession and the authorities would not investigate.

accounts.label: Denver Tribune wire
accounts.gist: Arrested and locked up at Otero, he was taken out when the mob broke into the jail Thursday night and strangled; the girl, Mary Butler, accused him of using morphine.

accounts.label: Trinidad dispatch
accounts.gist: Officials hurried him to Otero; the mob followed, forced the prison doors after nightfall Thursday and hanged him until he was strangled; chloroform was the drug named.

accounts.label: Kansas City Times special
accounts.gist: 'Dr. C. A. Woodburn' was hanged by the citizens at 9 o'clock on the morning of Dec. 2.

accounts.label: Indiana roundup version
accounts.gist: Miss Alice Sivel died of a morphine overdose while ill with pneumonia; Washington was arrested and discharged before a mob took him from jail.

framing.detail: The Las Vegas Morning Gazette called him a 'lustful wretch' and 'brute' and said 'it is a pity he isn't hung' before the lynching.
The Cheyenne Leader headed the Denver dispatch 'Served Him Right.'
The Denver Tribune, reprinted in Chicago, called it fortunate for the world that his life had ended 'even at the hands of a mob.'
National roundups ran a one-line notice among other crimes without comment.

info: Thursday night, December 2, 1880, in most reports; one dispatch says 9 a.m. on Dec. 2 and one roundup says the 3d
Otero, N.M., a railroad station on the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe about fifteen miles south of the Colorado line; one roundup says Raton
Dr. C. A. Washington (also 'Dr. A. C. Washington' and 'Dr. C. A. Woodburn'), a druggist and physician at Otero, said to be about 35 or 40; his race is not stated in any report
Accused in the dying statement of a hotel dining-room girl at Raton of drugging her with chloroform (or morphine) and assaulting her; she died Wednesday, Dec. 1
A mob, reported as following the officers from Raton to Otero; individuals not named
Body unburied when the train left; $629 reportedly found on it; his father-in-law arrived at Raton to take his effects
